title: Detecting one-dimensional bosonic SPT phases via twisted entropic order parameter
authors: Kosei Fujiki, Tsubasa Oishi, Soichiro Shimamori
abstract: Entanglement asymmetry, introduced by F. Ares, S. Murciano and P. Calabrese, provides a density-matrix diagnostic of symmetry breaking and successfully captures the Landau data associated with a broken symmetry pattern. However, it is by now well established that gapped quantum many-body systems can exhibit phases which are not characterized solely by Landau symmetry breaking. A fundamental example is a symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase, and the ordinary definition of entanglement asymmetry is insensitive to this topological information. In this work we introduce a refined quantity, which we call the twisted entropic order parameter, designed to detect SPT phases from reduced density matrices, particularly focusing on one-dimensional bosonic systems. The key ingredient in our construction is an ancilla degrees of freedom that coherently records the untwisted state and the twisted state associated to a one-ended topological defect of unbroken symmetry, so that the enlarged density matrix retains the charge carried by the defect endpoint. We demonstrate our proposal in concrete lattice models and further generalize it beyond ordinary group symmetries, establishing its ability to diagnose SPT phases. This provides a first step toward a unified entanglement-asymmetry framework for diagnosing quantum phases of matter.
summary: The paper introduces the twisted entropic order parameter, a refined entanglement diagnostic, to overcome the limitations of standard entanglement asymmetry in characterizing Symmetry-Protected Topological (SPT) phases. By incorporating an ancilla degree of freedom, this parameter successfully extracts topological information—the endpoint charge—that is otherwise invisible, allowing for the precise classification of 1D bosonic SPT phases.
main_problem: Ordinary entanglement asymmetry fails to distinguish between different Symmetry-Protected Topological (SPT) phases that share the same symmetry-breaking pattern. The goal is to refine this diagnostic to detect the residual SPT data protected by the unbroken subgroup.
main_result: The twisted entropic order parameter successfully diagnoses SPT phases by probing the endpoint charge, which is invisible to standard entanglement asymmetry measures.
method: The authors introduce a twisted entropic order parameter by enlarging the system with an ancilla degree of freedom to coherently record the untwisted and twisted states associated with a topological defect.
model_or_system: The focus is on one-dimensional bosonic gapped phases exhibiting symmetry breaking $G 	o H$. The method is applied to lattice models, such as the clock-broken $Z_N$ cluster ladder model.
key_observables: The twisted entropic order parameter ($\Delta S_{	ext{twi}, g, \lambda}(A)$) and the associated endpoint charge $\epsilon_{\omega}^g(k)$.
important_parameters: The residual $	ext{H-SPT}$ class $[\omega] \in H^2(H, U(1))$ and the symmetry group structure ($G, H$).
main_assumptions: The method is most rigorously defined at a zero-correlation-length fixed point; the detection capability might fail for SPT phases with nontrivial Bogomolov multipliers.

paper_structure: The paper first establishes the failure of standard diagnostics, then introduces the twisted entropic order parameter using an ancilla degree of freedom to probe the endpoint charge. It provides concrete examples in 1D bosonic systems and generalizes the framework to detect residual SPT information.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful, entanglement-based diagnostic tool to probe subtle topological order in condensed matter systems, extending beyond simple symmetry breaking patterns.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic illustration of a symmetry-defect endpoint charge in one-dimensional bosonic SPT fixed points. When a half-infinite g-symmetry operator bUB g acts on an SPT ground state, its bulk action can be pulled through the state, leaving an endpoint operator V † g localized near the right boundary of region A. At a fixed-point representative, this reduction is exact, while for a generic state in the same phase, the endpoint operator is dressed quasi-locally. Under the readout symmetry bUA k (k ∈CH(g)), its endpoint operator transforms as (2.15).
